Another one - GBPUSD H1. I've been waiting for this one to trigger as I felt it would make a good example of a weak base failing - clearly not the case. I still think it's a 'bad-un' but even they work occasionally. So, what can I learn from this?

1. Should I have added more weight to the Drop aspect and the time taken to return? 2. Should I have ignored the fact that it looks like an upward trending channel on D1, just below a compression area with the possibility of a break from the top of the channel into weakness? 3. I could even notice that the top and bottom of the base are lower than in its predecessors, implying new selling blood!

If the RBD had occurred in the shadow of the compression I might have preferred this more, but in the end I think that used Supply levels and obvious Resistance lines would always turn me off to similar occurrences.

I've included D1 so you can see what else was on my mind while I was waiting....

Thanks in advance of any comments.

Hello mettafort,

Thanks for taking the time to respond, and please don't worry that in trying to help me you might cause offence. We're all here to learn and exchange ideas, and that requires us to be open minded and intellectually honest - ready to accept our mistakes and learn from them, adopt new ways when they are better than ours, and allow ourselves and others to challenge our thinking so we can increase our awareness. Anyway, my ways are mostly self taught: I really have no doubt there are holes in my logic that need filling and some wild and woolly ways that need taming

As I posted my original forum homework I reviewed my annotated GBPUSD H1 chart and saw my reference to D1, I realised I should back up the comment with a D1 chart showing what else was on my mind, soooo, the D1 chart was a little hurried: a rare moment of rush on my part. So I entirely agree with the sentiment you express on your D1 (and almost all of what you say on H4) and that would have been factored into my thoughts if I'd only looked further back in history when I was doing mine....:)

But the devil is always in the detail, and as this is a qualitative process I have to weigh up the pros and cons, then go with whatever seems most convincing (whether or not my thinking is right, is another matter entirely!): as my H1 chart shows, I had a mix of pros and cons from which to draw a conclusion (not all were marked for legibility reasons: I could gas on forever, as you're probably realising by now ).

I go with the quote, "History may not repeat itself, but it sure does rhyme", this translates into a bias towards the detailed information conveyed by the most recent Price Action over the 'haziness' of older levels - I take guidance from history, but I apply it in a modern context. (I really hope that makes sense!). I've added another two charts, after yours, with some very simple annotation on the first and the second one being my original homework for reference. In the end I guess it boils down to this for me, the history (when you look back far enough) was saying, "maybe look for shorts", and the detail was saying "but just not from this particular level"!

Once again, thanks for your help.

Spongy.

If this is parabolic, as it is in the middle drop – the one before the last, then that was a good sign theres still a chance of a further turn. I would agree that it seems price has hit this area of supply a lot, but looking for its source, I turn to the main HTF and that would be daily for me, and there the amount of supply is good. Spongy said: Should I have ignored the fact that it looks like an upward trending channel on D1, just below a compression area with the possibility of a break from the top of the channel into weakness?

I think you are spot on with this analysis – the channel top is right at a key D1 supply level. Turning was high probability/low risk.

Spongy said: I could even notice that the top and bottom of the base are lower than in its predecessors, implying new selling blood!

I think so too – market structure is showing some movement to find a lower level of value. When I look at that suspect basing area, what it primarily says to me is that there is no convincing footprint in the price action that tells me we are getting enough strength to push out and up over this key supply level just yet.

Take aways from looking at the DBR and RBD's:

1. When price moves away from a level, it doesnt matter how soon a re-test back into that comes, thats the highest probability trade because of the probability of unfilled orders resting there.

2. When price rallies back into a previous RBD, the supply that came from the D of that previous RBD was cause of a new area of supply to form that is slightly lower than the previous (often). This causes the lower market structure highs to form, because new levels of supply just below the previous market structure highs has formed, capping price from reaching higher levels. This works both ways, and is what seems to happen many times, not always.

3. Price seems clearer to me that it is always moving around to find piles of orders, and depending on the strength of moves away from those piles, we can reason better about what the probabilities are when price revisits and retests.

4. Wicks or tails mean at the point price reached that extent, there were S/D pushing price faster than the opposing direction, but then that move is overwhelmed by the orders that get touched and filled.

5. When resting orders sit at these levels, they only execute when market orders take them out, or other execution mechanics force those orders to move to market orders. It is still liquidity takers that must drive price through these levels.

6. When price breaks out of a recent high or base, it often returns on the other side and re-tests. Re-testing suggests a conscious act for price to go test a previous level. To me it seems like it is more a result of price bouncing away from supply and working its way back to value, but as it hits the demand that was strong enough to break those highs, thats were orders exist to give this level support. This is S/R in action.

I am sure theres much much more I have missed. But here is my next analysis.

MF

Bouncing around ideas and opinions is good, it's how we stretch those mental muscles.

Hopefully other readers don't think we've gone off-topic in the homework section: it's still about RBDs, just different interpretations of the same information, and by keeping the conversation here, hopefully everyone benefits - if it had taken place in a journal it might get overlooked! And apologies if you still think it belongs somewhere else - this will be my last post on this particular chart (no cheering please).

Anyway, I think I had a bit of a breakthrough after reading your last post, then going back to the chart to mark up some lines to reply. The following chart will make it all clear, but item 3 was my primary reason for anticipating a failure at the RBD - this was coupled with my opinion of the weakness of the Base itself when the internal structure was viewed, the purposeful looking D1 up-channel, and my poor opinion of what was above that many-tested Supply above the RBD.

For clarity, I would still anticipate failure of this particular RBD for the reasons stated, but I can see that the main thrust of my argument may be erroneous under other circumstances as the chart will show.

What will I do differently next time?

1. Be even more mindful of the distance that price moves away from the Resistance line each time it makes a serious move away (in the context of what you will see in the chart below), and thereby try to moderate my opinion of obvious Resistance lines being obvious traps 2. Be mindful to keep time away from a level in perspective with the distance of the move (time is always going to be a factor for me as it shows willingness to try and get somewhere) 3. Try not to peer too far into the future. The bottom of that D1 up-channel may well hold, but I won't know until it happens - price has to get down there first, and where better than from Supply? All the better if R:R is acceptable

4. I think the rest of what I did was good enough (even though I drew different conclusions from D1) and I'll continue to be open-minded

However, I'm still going to prefer new Supply to be at distinct price levels (whether higher or lower, just not the same ), like you, I like clean Price Action that looks like it's got a purpose rather than just milling about. Just as well price didn't do as I anticipated, else I would have missed an opportunity to learn something important!

Anyway, my chart is below your quote. I hope the comparison between left and right examples can explain how I see the lefthand one as highly prospective while the righthand one (our old friend) still remains too weak even though they are essentially the same, and even though I have identified potentially faulty thinking.

Right, I'm off to get a bottle of wine, I shall raise a glass to you. Thanks for taking the time to force me to challenge my point of view - I shall re-read your posts a couple of times while I enjoy a drink!

Regards.

Hello tradingjedi,

As well as identifying the RBDs and DBRs, you need to mark out at what level reactions occurred (if any), consider those that failed and what happened at the level afterwards. Maybe not to the same degree that mettafort and I have just done - we had a common interest but different perspectives to explore, hopefully to the benefit of everyone.

A long while back I was in a webinar and the speaker made an almost throw-away statement - which I'm sure sailed straight through most people, but which piqued my interest. It was in response to a question I don't recall, but the reply was, "Although we look at the same charts, we see different things". There was more to it than that, but pondering that statement allowed me to form many questions I didn't even know I needed to ask, then answer them to find more questions. It started me on a path of discoveries - still ongoing - that I doubt I would've walked otherwise. I won't expand beyond that, but what is interesting is that three people looked at roughly the same GBPUSD information and applied their logic to it: two of those people had entirely different opinions of the same RBD and one person ignored it altogether on their chart!

So, the benefit comes from the qualitative exercise:

1. What attracted you to this particular RBD or DBR?, what didn't you like? Was your opinion that it would work or not? (Your opinion, mind, not the benefit of 20:20 hindsight 2. What happened when price did return to the Base in each case? If it reacted, where (zoom in to the Base and root around)? If it didn't, is there anything that you can learn about it so you can spot a bad-un in the future (that's why we need to find good and bad examples)?

3. What happened later when price returned to the Base from the other side? Did it react or ignore it again? 4. Zoom out and look back in time, does that change your perception of your chosen examples or help understand why some worked or failed?

By going through this process on your charts you will better train your brain to spot and sort these patterns out, and assess the likely turning point within them so you can successfully reduce your exposure in the market (by this I'm sort of referring to R:R, but I'm also taking time into account). And if you keep hitting a wall in your understanding it will better help everyone else to offer suggestions or guidance.

You don't need to slap everything on the chart, just your main line of reasoning and points of interest, maybe a little bit of filler in the post, but in doing so you will accelerate your understanding.

BTW, why didn't you mark up that RBD?:)

Regards.

Spongy.

Tried my best to focus on key levels, flips and the way DBR et al formations cause subsequent reactions or affects on price later. On the H4 diagram there is a key drop in price which forms a base after a strong move down. This decision point becomes one to continue the down move, and then this area itself becomes a nice supply level. So the base DP provides an area of S or R depending on the move. Bases seem to form a key areas in history where either a S or D level has been known to be present. And even when a supply level at a basing is broken, subsequently when price falls back under again, it can continue to have the same supply pressure as it did once before. tail/wick into S/D for the first time, seems to suggest a high chance of a second attempt working next time - this chart has lots of double tests before price moves up or down.

I am aware of over-analyzing, but I get insights that take my understanding deeper every time I do this.
